blocks.x: I'm going to start with just asking you to give you a full name and the date and place of your birth.
Joseph Henry Lide, and I was born in Worcester, England on the 13th of July, 1934.
And what's your legal address now, Joe? I mean, where would you vote if you voted?

I don't have one. I don't have one. I was 21 when I was just before I left to come here, and I'm not a registered voter anywhere, but I guess I can register and vote in the British election when I get back this year.
Are you going back to Worcester?
No, to Northern Ireland. That's where my parents live now.
What town?
Belfast. Belfast. Yeah.
Now, when you, how long have you been here in this country?
About three and a half years.
Three and a half years.
Came in October 55. Uh-huh.
And when you came over, did you come directly to New Orleans?

Well, I dropped, I landed in Boston, third Count Basie there one night, my first night in America. Okay. And then I sailed down from Boston to New York on a freighter. And caught a little bit of music there. And caught a little bit of music there, not much. Okay. Played with Wild Bill. That was my, just about my second night in America. I played with Condon.
Oh, yeah? Yeah. At what place?
At the, it was his old club in the village. He moved, I think he moved uptown about a year ago, but this was at his old place.
The one that was named Condon?
Condon, Eddie Condon. It was about three blocks from Washington Square. I forget the exact address.
Who was in the band besides you and Wild Bill?
Well, Wild Bill, Pee Wee Russell, Cuddy.
Yeah, Cutshaw.

That's right. I know, I could tell you that, I forget, Wettling was on drums. No, was he, no, wait a minute, no, a younger chap. I heard him another time, he was on drums. No, it was a younger chap on drums. A colored bass player, fat fellow with a white goatee, and I think Schroeder on piano. I think that was it, and Condon didn't play it all the whole evening. Then I got the bus down here.
Yeah. Well, anyway, when you were home in Ireland, when you came over here, your purpose, I mean, you were going, you were coming to New Orleans with just those few little stop-offs.
That's right, yeah, I meant to come here, yeah. Yeah. The reason why I wanted to come is I read the book Jazz Ways, you know, that big book with all the pictures. Yeah, yeah.

And I was talking to somebody the other day, and they said that most people from other countries, and especially people from Britain, come over here with the purpose of coming to New Orleans, you know, figuring it's just real heaven for jazz and everything. And, well, what do you think about it? It's being a heaven.
Well, I can't say I've been disappointed. It's very different to what I had supposed it would be. I had no idea that there were four brass bands marching. Maybe more. I had no idea of that.
You just didn't know how many.

I knew the Eureka existed. That's the end of it. That was all I knew. I didn't even know they still marched. I had an idea that George Lewis and all played here. They weren't here. When I got here, they didn't get here for several months after I arrived, and they weren't all that good. I didn't think at the time. Of course, I've been initiated now to appreciate the finer points, I guess, by knowing what to listen for. You know, I was listening for a different thing when I got here.
Excuse me, what bands did bands or and, or whichever way it goes, and or, did you hear in your home? I mean, records mostly. I mean, you probably heard some bands.
Yeah, well, I don't know.
Did you sort of start getting a taste for it?

Well, the first record I ever heard that I could even class as jazz was Pee Wee Hunt's record, The 12th Street Rag, which came out when I was about 14. And that was the first time I ever noticed jazz, you know. And then I was in school in Ireland, in Belfast, in boarding school, and all we had to do was listen to records. And some fellows got interested in jazz. There's a band in Belfast. They're always, they were a Dixieland band, and they always got very offended when anybody ever mentioned the Dixieland revival, because they played straight through. They kind of copied the Muggsy records of the late 30s, and they never stopped through the entire war, right through to when I got interested, you see. And they played for our high school dances, so forth. Ken Smiley's band, he's since given up music and went into the newspaper business, and he was the guy that handled Louis' tour to West Africa. He's high up now in the newspaper business. He's quit playing the trumpet. He's a Belfast man. And they played, and the fellows who bought the records that I first listened to, this sounds like total recall, but I guess it's what you want. Whatever. Yeah. They used to listen to him. And they bought a lot of Chicago stuff, pretty indiscriminate taste in buying the music. You know, you'd get all kinds of bad stuff. But they bought all the Bunk records which were available in England at that time, all of them on HMV, and none of them available in this country at the present time, to my knowledge, or ever have been, recorded late after about 47, I think. 47. 46 maybe. I don't, I think more than 47. And all sorts of other stuff. Wingy Manone, that kind of thing, you know. Chicago stuff. Condon, they all bought the Condon records. And Bunny Berrigan playing I Can't Get Started. That's one of the first records I ever, you know. I would still like it as much as I did then. Sure. That kind of thing.
That's a good thing.

And I remember the fellow, the fellow, we had a little band in school, you know, and I played trombone on it at that time. I used to play trombone. And he, he liked to imitate Bobby Hackett, that kind of stuff, you know, sort of late Chicago smooth stuff. And we played the odd job, again, at high school dances. And I remember he played me a Bunk Johnson record once and I asked him about the clarinet player, Lewis, and he said, oh yes, Lewis. Never heard the name. I was very impressed that he knew the name of somebody else who wasn't listed on the label. He said, yes, very old style that. He said, it's not much good. Nothing to compare with Pee Wee or somebody like that, which sounds funny now. When you consider the amount of fuss made about Lewis and how Pee Wee's kind of fallen, fallen off. And I play, we had this little band, I played trombone with them. And then, and I, we, and the first band I ever heard was that Ken Smiley band, which is a pretty smooth band. I think it would have held up, it would have held up pretty well by any standards, you know. It was, it was good white Dixieland.
They just got sort of tired of playing or something?

No, they, no, they, it went on and on. The big, the good, the better fellas in the band dropped out because they got better jobs and left Belfast. Yeah. But you see, they were stuck in Belfast through the entire war years. There was a kind of a little jazz continuity going on in Belfast because there wasn't any war in Northern Ireland to speak of. There was no conscription, for instance. Yeah. You see. And there, but of course, if they'd gone to England to get better jobs, as they could have got, then they would have been drafted. So they stuck on there and played. And then when the war got over and they got too old to get drafted, then they went and got good jobs in England and were, well, like Smiley, I was saying, was posted to West Africa working for the Daily Mirror.
Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh, about the jazz in Ireland, do they have the same sort of set up that I read about and hear about in England, you know, little clubs where they, uh...

Well, not... You know what I mean? Yeah. Not... Not when I left. It wasn't as impressive as it was in London. One or two jobs, one or two little bands. The... At the time when I was in high school, and I left high school in 51, uh, they only had, to my knowledge, they only had, uh, Ken Smiley's band. And he left around that time and it was taken over by the trombone player, very good trombone player, called Jimmy Compton, and, uh, he was, uh, he's kept the band going and it's still playing now, to my knowledge. I can't think of any reason why it shouldn't, uh, why it shouldn't still be going. He was, of course, there was the same thing, Smiley and all were kind of high-class people, you know, they wore blazers and that, old-school blazers and nice accents and all, you know, and, uh...
Nothing dirty? Did they play any dirty type music?

No, no, more smooth. He liked to croon and that a little, you know, but it was like those Muggsy records. And then the trombone player was very like, I'm reminded of a parallel, it was very like the way The Last Straws is going now. This band I've been playing in, uh, they've been publicized as a society band and they've certainly got all their jobs as a society band through contacts rather than ability, I would say. I would suggest I don't, uh... And gradually the peasants are taking over. You see, the sort of people who I would say can play better but haven't got the social context and that's exactly what happened to, uh, uh, Ken Smiley's band. The tromboneist's name was Jimmy Compton. Now it's called Jimmy Compton. It's a Duxy Lion Pine. That's the way they talk over there. He had this pianist who's, uh, the pianist was a very good fella too. He was in the regular army in charge of training, uh, cadets. He got posted somewhere in England. And his pianist, this fella called Hoppy, uh, Hoppy Compton. And he was the fella who came to me and, uh, told me he wanted to be a trumpeter and play like Bix once. And I asked him, well, how was he getting on? I mean, what kind of trumpet did he have? He says, well, he didn't have a trumpet but, uh, it was a question of mind over matter. He said that, uh, Ravel and Tabusi were Bix's favorite, uh, composers and he was stashing up every Ravel and Tabusi disc he could lay his hands on. He was, that's about the angle, you know, but they, they had, it was a pretty good band.
You gotta have some kind of, you gotta have some kind of.
Sure, that was his idea. He played, he played very good piano but he was anxious to be refined about it, you know.
Was he the, uh, trombone player's brother?

That was it, that's right. Oh, it's a good band, it's still going, they play all kinds of jobs and they'll play, the idea with them was, I mean, they were a Dixieland band but they played sambas and rumbas and all the rest of it, whatever the dancers wanted. Which is what a real new audience band does, of course, I mean, whatever the music, whatever

the audience wants. They play for dancing and if it happens to come out of Dixieland, well, okay. That's right. If it doesn't, okay, you can still dance to it. But they, but it was, what, a six or seven piece of band?
That's right, seven, they had a guitar. Yeah. And the regular six, they didn't have a banjo.
Then, and then mostly instead of playing like the clubs in London and some of the other towns in England, they would just spot around like, you know, like spotting around here, huh?
Yeah, any kind of jobs.
Like that.

Yes, they'd play anywhere. Uh-huh. They had one regular weekly job on a Saturday night at the, uh, the, I forget the name of the damn school they played at. They played in the gymnasium. Um, the Royal Academy, Belfast Royal Academy, BRA, one of the biggest schools over there.
Uh-huh.

Uh, every Saturday, but they play anywhere. They've, they've been playing at the boat club. Uh, it's very different to some of the boat clubs I've played in over here. It's, it's not a big bar, you know, more like across, you know, kind of thing. Yeah. All the mill girls go over there. Belfast is an industrial town. Uh-huh. Oh, it's very different in Belfast, if you're interested. I mean, Belfast is kind of a backwater, but it's very different. The approach to jazz over there always seemed to me, this is before I left, it might have changed, but it always seemed to be, uh, much more like here in that they were anxious to satisfy the dancers, the people who paid their few shillings to get in at all costs, rather than having this big pretentious, uh, we're going to revive the original New Orleans jazz at all costs, even though nobody can, uh, put their finger on what the original New Orleans jazz is. I mean, London, of course in London you've got anything to satisfy all tastes, I suppose. Yeah. And I went to London, in my last year of high school, I went to London, I heard Ken Collier's band in 1949, the Crane River Jazz Band. Of course he, Ken Collier's got kind of a name, he came over here and all.
Yeah.

He came in 53. Uh-huh. 53. Yeah. Uh, stayed for a few months, I think. He had another cornet playing with him, uh, Sonny Morris. And he got Monty Sunshine, who in those days played his kind of steel clarinet that he'd seen a photograph of George Lewis playing, you know. He played in a metal one?
Yeah, that's right, metal.

And he played, tried to play, he used to play all, I remember I had an old record of Bunk playing Tishomingo blues on Brunswick and hear the Crane River band and they'd play every note identically, you know, an old clarinet phrase coming through. No drums, Collier was always very particular about drums, he said until he could find a drummer that was fit to play with a New Orleans band, he wasn't gonna have one. Well, here's the thing. It's a completely different thing. First of all, it's a foreign business in England. It's something from somewhere else. And it's not looked at. It's more for the kids of Kora, they like it. It's sort of the same kind of kids that would be going to hear a rock and roll band over here, I would say. But also it's culture. You get a lot more pretentious people writing little articles about jazz in the intellectual weeklies than you do in this country. You've got people like Henthoff and all that New York mob waiting to pounce on anything. In the little magazines, now and again, the New Yorker does something. Just how it started and everything. Well. Who do you saw?

Well, they, they had a, they had a festival in Cuba, which is very like Mardi Gras here, only it wasn't on Mardi Gras. It was on May the 1st, which is, and around that time, I believe the thing's been going on a month, mainly on weekends. Very like Mardi Gras here, only a little wilder. More frightening. Uh, like here, you're, if you're not with Zulu, all you got is a lot of drunk people wandering up and down with drinks in their hands. There, they were all seen to be dancing in the street, passed on, packed on mass, you know, I mean, like soldiers, tight as soldiers, very old streets of them, you know, doing the cha-cha-cha and, uh, hitting all sorts of things, you know, or everything you could hit. And, uh, they had a big parade, I think that since the revolution, they've been kind of scared that the tourist trade's falling off, you know, all the gambling casinos are empty and that. So, uh, the municipality of Havana invited, uh, representatives from, I think, every country in the hemisphere to, uh, come and have a representative of some kind of festival that, uh, those countries have, and they picked New Orleans to represent America, and Mayor Morrison went over with three bands. Ours was one of them. And, uh, uh, I used the last straws, you know, and Roy Liberto's band and, uh, uh, Hector Fontana's band. And, uh, we went over and we were supposed to portray a, uh, brass band, a Negro marching band, and, uh, they had about a dozen other people all dressed up as typical old New Orleans characters. Because, you know, it sounds corny, but it was pretty impressive for what they wanted. You know, it wasn't all like that. Uh, black, everybody had black face and somebody would have a basket of, uh, strawberries or selling firewood or something. I'm trying to remember some of the other things. Uh, and, uh, we, we all got very, uh, huffy and refused to black our faces and that, um, because we thought it would be in bad taste and so forth. But, uh, it was impressed on us that, uh, we were damn lucky to go over there by the woman that had nominated our band to represent New Orleans and so forth. So everybody swallowed their pride and black their face. My, my shirt still isn't clean yet. They told us it was washable and stuff, but it wasn't. And we, approximately, we rehearsed like mad trying to play like a New Orleans brass band, you know, wasn't quite the right lineup, but it, we, I think we did pretty well. I still, to see some photographs, they got it all televised. They got a film of it at WDSU. And, uh, they had this and a couple of floats and so forth and Vic Shiro on a horse representing somebody with a flag or something and presented the flag to the mayor of Havana. And, uh, had rather the big Rex floats and Roy La Bertana thing. And I think we did pretty well out of all the countries. We led the parade, but the, the only ones that I, I really remember seeing, things were a little confused towards the end of the parade, but the, the only ones I remember seeing after we'd got off the route, you know, the parade route with the Brazilians and they had some kind of troops that they had from, uh, their festival, they have a Mardi Gras in, uh, Brazil. Oh, they were wonderful. They had us beat. But we did pretty well. It was very interesting and everybody was very pleased about it. And this, they thought this was just it, you know. I really enjoyed it over there. They don't have much jazz over there. There's one place they've got so much of their own stuff that, you know, Yeah. You know, that, uh, more rhythmic stuff.
Uh, do they have a lot of steel bands there? Not. Or are they mostly further?

No, not that I, further south. More, not that I know of. And I don't get the idea that I went all around, you know, trying to find it. I just heard what they have. They have some nice little bands, you know, trio or a quartet with guitars and stuff. And one of those, you know, those steel basses that vibrate, you know, they're just a box with a little vibrating. Yeah. They had those, but they were singing all, um, Spanish type songs, Cuban type of songs, not like the Calypso. I was in Jamaica a year ago, two years, nearly, ooh, two years ago. And it was fantastic when you could, uh, get way out in the hills, you know, where they didn't have any electricity or anything. Miles out, practically the jungle, you know, people living in huts and all that. And every Saturday night they'd have a dance and they'd bring a jukebox that was run from a battery on the truck. And they'd have all the Fats Domino records, all the Elvis records, all that, you know, I went out there expecting to hear the real Calypso because they had a bit if you dug it out. Yeah, same trouble. It's always interested me the way those, all the different, uh, forms that that kind of music has taken around the Caribbean and around this city and in Mexico too.
Yeah.
Some fine instrument, instrumental playing in Mexico. Mariachis, you know, trumpets. Yeah. Beautiful stuff.
Uh, there's a proposed trip to Vienna. Oh yeah. And what, when is it?

Well, it's supposed to be in August and it's the, we're having a recording session tonight and, and that everybody's very excited about it, but it still doesn't seem to be definite. The idea is, uh, we're not going to get paid for it as we were not paid in Havana, just the same, but we got our, or the whole trip paid in Havana. And I don't know whether we're going to be able to get, uh, the band's going to be able to get its trip paid to Vienna. I'm, uh, I'm going to be in Europe myself. I'm leaving next Friday, leaving town next Friday and sailing on Monday. Uh-huh. Uh, that's what we're going to decide tonight. I think it's, I think it's a very good chance of us going at the moment, play for this communist youth festival in Vienna. It's the first time they've had the festival outside the Iron Curtain, you see, in the American youth organization. I forget what the name of it is. He's very anxious to get as many people to go voluntarily. Uh-huh. You know?
I saw something in the paper a few days ago. That's right. Yeah. A letter from a member or perhaps some officer in a local American. American Legion. Yeah. You saw that.

Yeah, but also there's, there was, I read the paper today, there's an article, um, that the American Legion have offered to help the organization now and acquaint them with communist tactics. Yeah. Something like that. I don't know. I didn't get, I don't think there ought to be too much to worry about. Of course, I hope we're not there when, you know, there won't be any trouble. I don't see why they should. Everybody was pretty scared that we'd get shot in Havana. There was people wandering around with Tommy guns, you know. Yeah. We survived.
Uh, when you go back, when you go back home, Joe, are you going to teach?

Yeah. Probably. I want to also do a bit of studying on my own, you know, mark time without having the pressure on. Yeah. And I want to play a little too, I suppose. Of course, I don't know what the situation is over there. It's three years since I've been there. It might be so much that everybody's fed up with it or, I don't know, I have an idea that might be. On the other hand, I might be able to, to play. I'd like to start a brass band if they got one brass band, I mean, I think another one could help. Sure, they got several here, whatever.
Sure. They have a couple or three there.
And I've played with the Eureka over here. Learned a little bit about it. I mean, they used to play slowly, much slowly. Yeah.
I know that you played, you played Mardi Gras Day.
Yes, that's right.
So, what would you call that? A walk-in? You were just walking in there?

That's right. Well, I've played with the Eureka before. The first time I ever played with them was Mardi Gras last year, not this year. 58, I just played one number. Everybody was loaded, you know, and Sheik wanted to rest, you see. Oh, it was late in the day. And then I played a big parade across the river, which was one of those parades where you go from everybody, different houses and have lots of drinks and that. I think it was the Young Men Olympians, I forget which one. Every time I go over there now, everybody claims that I was in their house drinking, but I don't think I was in that many houses. And then I played, Paggio had a big sore on his lip the size of a penny, this Mardi Gras. And I played for his trumpet for three or four hours. Oh, I got so tired. Played from about noon until the rain came on. You remember the storm hit?
I left before. You mean on Mardi Gras day with the Zulus?
Yeah, that's right. I left before.

Before that. I never can. I think I last... Two or three hours. I started, no, I started Eads Plaza and I get to La Salle just off Jackson. And then I'm just about pooped, so I usually leave by then. And that's only maybe an hour.

I stuck with him from nine till four. And then recently I played Arthur Ogle's Funeral. You know, he, um, he's an old drummer of the Eureka. He's on the Pax record and he had both his legs amputated before I even got to town. He died about a month ago and I played, uh, there was no money involved in it and she asked me to play. Uh, Percy couldn't make it. And, uh, Bokaj couldn't, Bokaj wasn't there and Jim Crow couldn't make it. He was playing with the Eureka at that time. He, somebody had to fix his TV set or something. So he had to stay at home and Red Clark couldn't make it. And the drummer they couldn't get in touch with. So he was just about a pickup band. Paul Barberin played bass drum. They got him at the last minute. And Kid Howard joined us halfway through. The funeral was in the church right opposite the bar where Howard drinks. Right there. You know where it is on, uh, Liberty, very close to the Civic Auditorium where Jim Robinson lives and Sonny Henry lives there too. Howard lives there. They all live just on that corner.
I don't know. Sonny lives downtown, I think.

That's right. By the Civic Auditorium. Oh yeah, yeah. It's on, it's Liberty is it or someone or something. And anyway, I don't know. On Marais. St. Philip. Yeah, somewhere around Marais and St. Philip. Or Liberty and St. Philip.
So close to the, uh. Rampart. Caledonia. That's right. Well now. Is that the bar?

Yeah, that's not the bar where they drink, but that's where we finished up. We played, uh, it was a very short funeral and played a couple of, uh, spirituals, not dirges. I can't play dirges. I can play spiritual slowly. And, uh, then we marched back to the Caledonia Inn and then we all went in there and played, oh, for about an hour. Uh huh. Just playing, you know, just for kicks, because somehow nobody was getting paid so nobody seemed to care. And all the people at the Eureka who were sort of in command, they were the ones that, uh, couldn't make it. So, nobody seemed to mind. That was very pleasant.
Yeah.
That's the only funeral I've ever played. 된 stuff with

Of course I doubt if the practice of playing music at funerals can be revived in England if they ever had it. And I've enjoyed playing with them of course much more than playing with this little band up here, which is nice but which is still a little bit rushed, you know, still confusing speed with heat. And it affects one's own playing. If you play with good people then you tend to play better I think than if you're not. The same thing I was saying about the paddock, a lot of it's what you expect is demanded of you.

You're playing, I'm just thinking of the way you sound. I have a pretty definite idea about maybe the trumpet player that you like the most. Would you say that there's any trumpet player that you like the most? Well I like... I don't mean just playing here, I mean any player.

Well I say I like Percy Humphrey the most but I don't think I manage to sound very like him. I think I sound like, more like Wild Bill every time I hear the playbacks. But I don't really want to, I don't know why I do. I listen to him a great deal, you know, a lot. Oh I'd like to play like the punk, if I could. Very sort of simple, very simple, very swinging.
You remind me in your playing, or maybe the way you're phrasing, I think of Louie a lot.
Oh I wouldn't say that.
Well I didn't.

You think so? I don't know. Everybody's influenced by Louie to a certain extent. I mean all of them but I couldn't approximate any, I would never get close to the way he played in the 20s, you know, hot fire.
I don't mean that you, I think that you come up to his greatness or anything like that. I mean just sort of the feeling of it. Well maybe so. Maybe it all came out of the same, same bunch of guys.

Yeah, I listened, yeah well that's right. If you listen to anybody who played after Louie you tend to, tend to get a lot of Louie through that too. Yeah, yeah, that's right. Though I don't think Percy, that's the thing. I mean, if ever you can sort of pin down an influence of everybody. I mean you can sort of say, well, Bunck's one of the originals and maybe Joe Oliver is and then Louie sort of followed them but he's an original too. And then after that, everybody built on that. But Percy I can't pin down, I can't think where he got that style. I think he's an original too. Which is...
He could very well be.

Which is mainly the attraction for him. Somebody once called me, I don't know, some fool around here. Forget who it was. He was telling me once I was talking about the Eureka or something saying I was a jazz snob. Because I only wanted to listen to the older stuff, you know. Well, I wouldn't call it that. I'd call it, if you're going to put a term to it, I'd call it being a jazz antiquarian. Which I'm not. But there's something, you know, there's something really nice about a man who's, I think I said, about Percy who's playing in his own field in this sort of New Orleans brass band field and yet it's completely original, completely fresh. Lovely tone and all the lovely fresh phrasing. I've never heard anything like it. I don't know anybody that imitates him. Maybe Ken Collier tries a little. He played with the Lewis band when Percy was leading it. When he was over here in 53. That's who I'd like to sound like, but that sounds ridiculous trying to, saying you'd like to sound like somebody. You see, that means you're...
You were mentioning Collier's sounding, what, 1949 sounding like an intentionally copy... From Bunk. From Bunk.

Yeah, well, the band was sort of meant to be like Bunk. See, George and Jim Crow both play in styles which I gather is fairly easy to imitate, even if not to, you know, to make it sound like the same, not have the same swing. And it's sort of basically simple stuff. I mean, it's much easier to copy George, I would think, than to copy, I don't know, Johnny Dodd. Nobody would copy Johnny Dodds. But George, you know, I mean, anybody can get that. You know, I can't say this, I can see, they're going to have to edit all this like mad. But anyway, they tried, they tried to imitate George's style. They still do, like mad, everyone wholesale. And that's what they tried to do. Collier, I don't think, ever sounded much like Bunk. He tried to sound like every record he ever heard. He got a bit of Mutt Carey and he got a bit of Percy Humphrey after he got back to, back from New Orleans. And Russell once pointed out to me that what he didn't like about Collier was that he tried to imitate the bad stuff as well as the good stuff. He'd take a record with Kit Howard playing when his lip was terrible, the notes weren't even, you know, the notes were wavering. And Collier would think that was vibrato and very high class and try to play that. And he's got a record of himself doing that. I think that's why Russell doesn't approve him too much. And I think he's largely justified. Except that Russell's one of the few of us who's ever heard the really good men when they were really good. And so he's on an eminence where we have to make do with what we've got, especially if you're stuck in England. And at the time I left England there wasn't any American jazz allowed over there. I mean the Lewis band has been over there a couple of times I think now, but at that time the union was in some terrible deadlock and nobody was allowed to go over there. Cal Collier was filling some kind of a gap. People couldn't even buy most of the records. They're unavailable over there. Still are, the American music records.
Still what?
Still unavailable over there. They got pirated now and again.
Yeah, that's what I heard.

I didn't think all that much of Bunk until I heard Russell's records, until I got over here and heard the American music records. I thought he was just a pretty player, but they were made towards the end, when the band was kind of splitting up, I think.

it's just the fashion whatever is a fashion that's okay that's right that's terrible
And jazz doesn't seem to be the fashion much here, does it? I mean, you don't get too much of it.

The kids don't seem to like it. There was some talk of our little Dixieland band catching on. We played at Newman High School a couple of times, but the trouble is the kids can't dance to it. Until Dixieland imitators can learn how to play for dancing, they'll never be playing real jazz. You're playing so fast, you know.
Yeah, if you could play Dixieland and still play it with a sort of a rock and roll feel, you'd get a lot of fun, and you can do it.
You can do it.
You can play it all.

I wouldn't be surprised if that wasn't the kind of thing that Bolden... You talk to somebody like Peter Boccage, you know, he says that Bolden played just, you know, nothing but the blues, strictly lower class people, no musical imagination. Well, that sounds like rock and roll to me. Of course, it's not the same, you know, electric guitars and all that, but that's probably more of the spirit. People like to go and dance to it. Boppy music. That's right. Oh, it's a shame to see those poor little high school girls just in their first high heels practically trying to dance to the speed we play at.
Yeah.
But you can't tell them. You can't tell them. They've slowed down a bit since they marched in Havana. You know, it's possible to play hard, you know,
when you've got the physical effort of walking, holding you back from speeding up,
and you can still play well.
You mentioned that when you leave here Friday that you won't be sailing until Monday. Monday, Diamond.

Good. I spent a couple of nights in New York, see if I can catch any music. I don't know. I was looking at the New Yorker, but I don't see too much on it. I'd like to hear some of the modern bands, you know, I mean, there's some who are interested in that as well.
You know, I hear that some of the modern, some of the extreme moderns, like I believe Monk is interested in recording Jelly Roll tunes.
Yeah?
I didn't know that. And Jimmy Jufri has made some things, I think he's now playing Santa Claus blues,
Yeah.
Things like that, but with a modern...
Well, Jelly was a great composer, wasn't he?
Sure he was.
Some great tunes.
Sure.
I know Wally Stavenport's interested in starting a brass band.
Really?

With a slightly modern... Yeah, if he can, he doesn't know much about it, but he's interested in the idea. Bob Reinders was telling me that there were some kids that he was teaching out at Xavier, coloured kids, a young, you know, the younger generation, which, you know, are lacking really in the brass band business. They were interested in not letting it die, but somehow the idea fell through.
Well, at least there's an interest.

Sure. I think this business of letting the brass bands getting sort of... Some of the instrumentalists being more modern within the frame of brass band music is the inevitable thing, and I think it's better than nothing. Far better than nothing. Oh, yeah. Got to have it.
Oh, the tuxedo is so much different from the U.A., but they still go.

Sure, sure. It's just a different style. They don't sound... Yeah, they... You know, it's... They just had a little bit more control, all those discordant notes at the end, you know, like on the record. Everybody seems to be finishing in a different key. Yeah. But that's the... That's the... That's the... That's the... That's better than just letting it finish completely.
Sure.
Which is what the... You get the idea it might do that if... You tell everybody off who wants to play a modern phrase. Yeah. Yeah. And you tell them...
Yeah. Yeah.
And you can... I mean, I think it's mainly a question of taste rather than ability, as I think I said, and you can play modern and still be very tasteful. Oh, sure.
As far as I'm concerned.
Sure.
Since you played in high school, you said you started that way, then you read songs.
Not at sight. Not at sight. I can read if I figure it out.

segments.title: Birth, address and arrival in America in 1955
segments.summary: Joe Lyde gives his name, birth in Worcester in 1934, parents in Belfast, and arriving in the US in October 1955.

segments.title: Landing in Boston and playing at Eddie Condon's club in New York
segments.summary: On his first nights in America he hears Count Basie in Boston and sits in with Wild Bill Davison at Condon's club, then takes the bus to New Orleans.

segments.title: Why he came to New Orleans and what he found
segments.summary: He came after reading Jazzways; he was surprised by the number of brass bands and that George Lewis was not yet in town.

segments.chapter: Growing up with jazz in Belfast
segments.title: First jazz records and the school band in Belfast
segments.summary: Pee Wee Hunt, Bunk Johnson and Condon records, a school band on which he played trombone, and Ken Smiley's Belfast band.

segments.title: Jimmy Compton's Belfast Dixieland band and its members
segments.summary: Belfast's small wartime jazz scene, the polite society band, its members, and the dance jobs it played.

segments.chapter: Growing up with jazz in Belfast
segments.title: Where the Belfast band played, and Belfast's approach to jazz
segments.summary: Belfast's small wartime jazz scene, the polite society band, its members, and the dance jobs it played.

segments.chapter: Growing up with jazz in Belfast
segments.title: Traditional versus progressive in England, and the Graham Bell tour
segments.summary: Whether English traditional players move on to modern styles, a Tuxedo parade he heard, and the touring Australian band.

segments.chapter: Growing up with jazz in Belfast
segments.title: Learning trombone and buying a cornet at school
segments.summary: He played trombone and cornet in the school band at Campbell College and bought a secondhand cornet at 16.

segments.title: Coming to Tulane as a graduate student and teaching
segments.summary: He came to Tulane on an English scholarship and has taught for three years.

segments.title: The Eureka Brass Band: first funeral and Percy Humphrey
segments.summary: He recalls his first Eureka funeral, praises Percy Humphrey and the bass drum, and talks about Eureka personnel.

segments.summary: He discusses British jazz fashion, writers and clubs that do not serve alcohol.

segments.title: The 1959 Havana festival trip with the Last Straws

segments.chapter: Playing in New Orleans and influences
segments.title: Playing Arthur Ogle's funeral with a pickup band
segments.summary: A pickup Eureka band played the drummer's funeral and then jammed at the Caledonia Inn.
